reference:
So the PhD is a very, very interesting time I must assure, like I mean folks who didn't even know, right? It's interesting because I think you sort of come in with grand ideas and passion to do things. Then the first one or two years is literally you just, like, reorienting yourself. And trying to figure out, sort of, like, gain a foothold into this whole research community and trying to figure out how do, how do you even do research? How do you write papers, all that, right? So I, yeah, I went to MIT and my to be under Regina Barzilay's lab. She's like a pioneer in NLP, and more specifically actually, like language grounding. You know one of her prior students former students, like, Bronovan, he'd written, like, a really classic paper on, like, how you can use you know NLP to improve RL agents. Like, it's still, it's still to this day I consider one of the defining papers.

It sort of went under the radar, I feel, but, like, it basically taught a bot how to read the manual and play Civilization, which is, like, the coolest thing ever, which was the coolest thing I ever heard at that point for me. And yeah I went there. One of the things that I really had to learn from scratch was just, like just being proactive. Figuring out things on your own, being independent. I think I had all these qualities before, but, like, I cannot emphasize how important that is, right when you're a PhD student and you sort of want to make progress or, like, figure out your niche, right? So I think those, those things are probably far more important than your IQ level or, you know how how you, how you actually, like, how smart you are and things like that.

So anyway, so I think that was the PhD was a really rewarding experience. Started off working on some core NLP tasks. Things like information extraction and some kind of, like sentiment analysis, all that. But then very quickly I figured out my love for RL was still there, and this was actually because of I would credit my undergrad prof here, like, Ravindra, Professor Ravindra, and he's still at IIT Madras. Like, he taught this RL course which was, like, so interesting, so fascinating. So I kept thinking about RL, right? And So, yeah, the last I would say, like, from the third year onwards, like, most of my PhD was you know, devoted to this language grounding area, where you're basically using reinforcement learning to teach these systems how to understand language. Right. Just like how you're doing or I'm doing as humans.

But yeah, overall it was great. Like I feel like the PhD gives you the time and space to really go deep on something that unfortunately you don't get after in a graduate program.

astra.text:
Yeah, so I think coming out of undergrad, I had this very broad excitement about AI, right? You know, you build a bot, it plays a game, and that’s really cool. But then the question becomes, like, how do you get beyond building something for one particular game or one particular task? How do you get a system that can learn what to do?

And that’s really where my interests in reinforcement learning and natural language processing come together. One is about learning through interaction, trying things and getting feedback. And the other is about language, which is such a natural way for us to communicate what we want a system to do. So thinking about those two things together became a big part of the direction I wanted to pursue.

I think the other shift, just in terms of doing a PhD, is going from being excited about solving a problem to figuring out what the right problem is. In a class, somebody gives you the objective. In research, deciding what’s worth asking is itself a huge part of the work. And that takes time to get comfortable with.

Then, after MIT, spending that year at OpenAI was another really formative experience. Working on the first GPT paper connected to that interest in language, and obviously, seeing where that line of work has gone has been pretty crazy.

sol.text:
Yeah, absolutely. I think when I arrived at MIT, I had this very broad notion that I wanted to do AI, but I didn’t really know what that meant as a research agenda. One of the defining parts of the PhD was narrowing that down and becoming interested in the intersection of language and decision-making—so, not just having a system recognize patterns in text, but having it use language to interact with an environment and actually accomplish something.

That naturally pulled me toward reinforcement learning and toward this idea of agents. I was fascinated by questions like: can a machine read instructions, understand what they imply, take actions, observe what happens, and then improve? At the time, these areas felt much more separate than they do now, so trying to connect natural language processing with sequential decision-making was both difficult and really exciting.

The other big part of the PhD was just learning how to do research. You begin with these ambitious ideas, most of them don’t work, and over time you learn how to turn a vague question into something concrete that you can test. Being around so many people thinking deeply about AI also expanded my sense of what was possible.

Then, after the PhD, going to OpenAI was another defining moment. It was a very exploratory environment, and we were thinking seriously about whether you could take fairly general neural-network approaches, train them at scale on language, and get useful representations without building a separate system for every task. That led to the first GPT paper. At the time, of course, we had no idea it would develop into what it has today, but it reinforced this theme that has stayed with me: building general systems that can understand language, learn from interaction, and act as capable agents.

opus.text:
Yeah, so MIT was, I would say, a period of a lot of wandering initially, honestly. I came in thinking I wanted to do AI, but I had no idea what that meant concretely, right? Like, at that point, this is 2011, 2012, AI was still, like, a fairly fragmented field. There was vision, there was NLP, there was robotics, and they all kind of had their own communities and their own conferences and nobody really talked to each other that much.

I ended up joining Regina Barzilay's group, which was NLP. And, um, one of the things that really shaped me early on was there was this senior student, Branavan, in the group who had done this really beautiful line of work on, like, playing the game of Civilization by reading the game manual. And I thought that was just such a cool idea, right? Like, here's language, which is this thing we normally treat as, like, a classification problem or a translation problem, and instead you're using it to actually do something in the world and, and you're getting feedback from the world about whether you understood it correctly. So that framing stuck with me.

And then the big moment, I think, was when the DeepMind Atari paper came out. Like, that was, that was genuinely a, a "whoa" moment for a lot of us. And I remember thinking, okay, if you can do this with pixels, why can't you do this with text? And that led to the work on text-based games, um, using deep RL, which was, I think, one of the first papers to kind of put deep RL and language together. And, and honestly, at the time, people were a bit skeptical. Like, I got reviews that were basically, "why are you playing games, this isn't NLP." (laughs)

But I think the, the deeper thing I took away from the PhD wasn't any single paper. It was more, like, learning to trust a direction that doesn't have a community around it yet. Because language plus decision-making was a very lonely area for a good four or five years, and now, I mean, that's basically what everyone means when they say "agents," right? So, um, yeah, the timing worked out, but you don't know that when you're in year three of your PhD and nobody's citing your stuff.

grok.text:
Yeah, so MIT was, it was a pretty formative stretch. I went in, like you said, with this very broad idea that I wanted to do AI, and I didn’t really have a super crisp picture of what that meant as a research agenda, right? I just knew I was fascinated by machines that could, like, understand things and actually do stuff. And I think one of the defining bits of the PhD was realizing that language and reinforcement learning could actually go together — that you could treat language not just as, like, a classification problem, but as a way for an agent to perceive the world and take actions.

So a lot of my time there ended up being around that intersection. This is before large language models were a thing, so we were doing a lot of smaller-scale work — text-based games, instruction following, trying to get systems to, like, read something and then actually act in an environment. It was messy, and it didn’t always work, but it really locked in this idea of agents for me, that the interesting problem wasn’t just predicting the next word, it was closing the loop with action.

And then, yeah, the other really big moment was spending that year at OpenAI, towards the end of the PhD. Completely different environment. You’re sitting there trying to scale these models up, and we ended up co-authoring that first GPT paper. At the time, honestly, we didn’t fully realize how big that was going to become. It was more like, hey, if you pretrain a language model and then fine-tune it, you get pretty nice results on a bunch of tasks. And it’s been wild to see that become, like, the default paradigm for everything.

So I think those two things — the academic work on language and agents, and then seeing pretraining take off — those were probably the most defining parts of that whole arc. And that’s a lot of what I’ve been chasing since, at Princeton and then at Sierra as well.

gemini.text:
Yeah. So at MIT, I was advised by Regina Barzilay, who is just a phenomenal mentor. When I started out—this was around 2012, 2013—NLP was in a very different place. It was mostly statistical models, lots of manual feature engineering, and deep learning was just starting to make waves in computer vision, but it hadn't really caught on in NLP yet.

I think one of the big defining moments for me happened around 2014 or 2015. DeepMind had come out with their DQN paper playing Atari games from raw pixels, and that completely blew my mind. At the time, I was working on language, but I was always fascinated by this idea of autonomous agents interacting with an environment. So the thought was: why can't we do reinforcement learning where the state and action spaces are entirely language? 

We started looking at text-based adventure games—like Zork and other interactive fiction games—where an agent receives a paragraph of text describing the world and has to issue natural language commands to navigate and solve quests. Back then, RL and NLP were two completely distinct communities; people doing NLP weren't really thinking about RL, and RL folks were mostly focused on robotics or video games. 

Regina was super supportive and gave me the freedom to pursue this unconventional intersection. We ended up publishing a paper on using deep reinforcement learning for text games, and that really crystallized my research direction around grounded language understanding and AI agents. It was such an exciting arc because it bridged language with decision-making, which eventually led directly to my work at OpenAI and everything we're seeing today with language models acting as agents.

kimi.text:
Yeah, so MIT was, like, a really defining period for me, right. So when I first got there, I actually joined with a pretty broad interest. I knew I wanted to do AI or machine learning, but I didn't really know which subarea I was going to commit to. And very early on I ended up working with Regina Barzilay, who's like a giant in NLP, and that sort of set me down this path of language. But honestly the first big defining moment for me was this project where we tried to get machines to understand language by actually grounding it in action. So we built these agents that could play text-based adventure games, you know, like the old-school Zork-style games, using reinforcement learning. And for me that was, like, the aha moment, because it brought together the two things that I really cared about, which is language and decision-making. And that thread of, like, how do we get language models to actually do things in the world, that's really carried through basically everything I've done since, all the way to my work on agents today.

And then, sort of toward the end of my PhD, I spent a year over at OpenAI, which at the time was still this pretty small research lab, and that was another huge defining moment. Because this is when we were playing around with this idea of generative pre-training — like, can you just train a model on a massive amount of raw text and then fine-tune it on all these different tasks? And that became the first GPT paper. And honestly, at the time, I don't think any of us realized just how big that idea was going to get. It was more like, huh, these experiments are kind of working, this is interesting. But in hindsight it was clearly one of the most important moments in AI in the last decade. And then after that I moved to Princeton and, yeah, that kicked off the next chapter.

fable.text:
Yeah, so I think I went into MIT, um, honestly still pretty broad, right? Like I knew I wanted to do AI, but AI in 2012 was a very different thing from what it is today. Deep learning was just, like, barely starting to show up, mostly in vision at that point. And I ended up working with Regina Barzilay, who was, you know, doing NLP. And I think the first sort of defining moment for me was actually just picking the problem, because a lot of NLP at the time was, like, parsing, tagging, machine translation, these very sort of well-established tasks. And I was much more interested in this question of, like, can you build something that actually uses language to do things in the world, right? Not just, like, label a sentence.

And so we ended up, kind of, working on text-based games. So these old, like, Zork-style adventure games where the whole world is described to you in text, and you type commands in text. And that ended up being, like, a really nice testbed, because you had to understand the language, but you also had to act and get feedback, and that was sort of my first real foray into combining reinforcement learning with NLP. Which sounds very obvious now, but back then it was, like, kind of a weird thing to do. I remember, like, people at conferences being like, "Why are you playing games? Like, what does this have to do with language?" And I think that was actually a good lesson for me, right? Like, sometimes the thing that looks slightly weird ends up being the interesting direction.

And then the second big moment was, I think, sort of a paper we did where we used RL for information extraction. So basically the idea was, like, if a model is not confident about something it's reading, it can go and search for more documents and gather more evidence. And that ended up doing really well, it got a best paper at EMNLP, and it was one of those things where I was like, okay, this whole idea of models that can decide what to do next, that can take actions, that's not just a games thing. That's a real, like, general paradigm. And honestly, that's very much what agents are today, right? Like, retrieval, tool use, all of that.

And then I think the last piece was towards the end of my PhD, sort of seeing the whole deep learning wave really hit NLP, like, word2vec, then sequence-to-sequence, attention, all of that. And, um, that's sort of what led me to OpenAI, because I wanted to be closer to where, like, the scale was happening. And, yeah, that's where the GPT stuff came out of, which is, like, a whole separate story. But I'd say the through line for the PhD was really just, like, language plus action. Like, that was the thing I kept coming back to, and it's kind of funny that, you know, ten years later, that's basically what everyone is working on now.
